name: Tropicarium – The “Shark Zoo”
description: Tropicarium, known as the Shark Zoo, is a marine and tropical aquarium inside the Campona Shopping Center in Budapest's 22nd district. Opened in May 2000, it has eight halls, sand tiger and brown reef sharks seen from a 12-metre tunnel, a ray pool and a rainforest section with alligators.

children.text: Tropicarium is an aquarium and animal exhibition inside the Campona Shopping Center, at Nagytétényi út 37-43 in Budapest's 22nd district. It opened on 26 May 2000. The official site calls it one of the largest marine aquariums in Central Europe, and a history page for the attraction gives its size as almost 3,000 square metres. It is a different venue from the zoo in City Park and from the similarly named Tropicarium in Kolmården, Sweden.

The concept goes back to Károly Farkasdi, a Hungarian businessman living in Sweden, who with his family created a first establishment of this kind in Kolmården in 1990. The Budapest project followed: construction began in September 1999 and took eight months. A visitor guide says the build used hundreds of tons of concrete and iron, with filtration and purification systems, and that most of the decoration was handcrafted by Tropicarium staff.

The exhibition is arranged in eight halls with hundreds of species. They include a Hungarian fauna section, freshwater and saltwater tanks, a coral reef, a reptile and insect house and a rainforest with alligators and dwarf caimans, where a tropical rain shower falls above the alligator enclosure every 15 minutes. Monkeys and snakes are also kept.

The headline attraction is the shark aquarium, with sand tiger and brown reef sharks, which visitors can watch from a 12-metre viewing tunnel running beneath it. A ray pool lets visitors touch and feed rays under staff guidance. Feeding days are set by animal group in the official schedule, so check the site if you want to see a particular feeding.

The operators have said they add one or two new aquariums or terrariums at a time so that returning visitors find something new, and a page last updated in 2010 reported nearly four million visitors in about eight years. The attraction is described as wheelchair and stroller accessible, and a cloakroom is available because the indoor air is warm.
Good to know
Check the official Tropicarium site for current opening times and tickets, and for holiday arrangements.
Tropicarium is inside the Campona Shopping Center in the 22nd district, outside the centre; plan the journey with a public transport planner or check the shopping centre's directions.
Flash photography is not allowed, and visitors cannot re-enter the exhibition once they leave it according to the site.
Guided tours in Hungarian and English must be booked in advance by email.

historyIntro: Tropicarium grew out of a concept first built in Sweden in 1990 and opened in Budapest on 26 May 2000, inside the Campona Shopping Center, after eight months of construction.

children.text: A history page for the attraction credits the concept to Károly Farkasdi, a Hungarian businessman who lived in Sweden between 1963 and 1998. In 1990 he and his family created the first such establishment in Kolmården, Sweden. The Budapest aquarium is a separate venue from the Swedish one.

Intensive construction began in Budapest in September 1999 and took eight months. A visitor guide says the work involved hundreds of tons of concrete and iron, filtration, purification and IT systems, and that most of the decoration was handcrafted by Tropicarium staff. The facility opened on 26 May 2000 in the Campona Shopping Center, on the outskirts of the city, and was described as the largest sea aquarium in Central Europe at almost 3,000 square metres, arranged in eight rooms.

The history page says the operators add one or two new aquariums or terrariums at a time to give returning visitors something new. About eight years after the opening, they reported nearly four million visitors. That page was last updated in 2010, so later developments are not covered there. Check the official site for the present exhibits, which include sand tiger and brown reef sharks and a 12-metre viewing tunnel.

name: Óbuda Museum
description: The Óbuda Museum sits in an outbuilding of the baroque Zichy Mansion on Fő tér. Its permanent exhibition, Óbuda - Three Faces of a Town, follows the district from its medieval royal days to the 1970s, with period scenes such as a manor salon, a cooper's workshop and a small inn.

children.text: The Óbuda Museum is at Fő tér 1 in Óbuda, the old town on the Buda side of the Danube that was once a royal centre. It is part of the Zichy Mansion complex, a one-storey baroque building built for Count Miklós Zichy between 1746 and 1752 according to the Kassák Museum, which occupies the main house. Renovation of the complex began in 2008, and the museum's own description says the building's design was matched to the design of the square.

The permanent exhibition, Óbuda - Three Faces of a Town, covers the district from the Middle Ages to the 1970s in three units. The first presents medieval Óbuda when it was a royal centre. The second covers the village-like small town from the Zichy era to the early 20th century. The third shows the demolition of older buildings, the rebuilding of the area and the social changes that came with it.

The exhibition includes hands-on activities, tasks and recreated scenes. According to the museum, visitors walk in over cobblestones that link past and present, and rooms include a manor-house salon with Miklós Zichy, the workshop of the cooper Simon Tóbiás and a small inn. An English-language audio guide is available.

An older museum helps explain the name. The first local and settlement museum of Budapest opened in Óbuda in 1927 in an old boys' school as the Árpád Museum of Óbuda, but its collection was lost in the Second World War. The current museum is not its successor and regards itself only as its spiritual heir.

The surrounding complex is useful context. The outbuildings also contain the Vasarely Museum, and the Térszínház and Hello Wood workshops, while the Kassák Museum is in the mansion. The Óbuda Museum also runs other sites in the district, including the Goldberger Textile Collection on Lajos utca.
Good to know
Check the official Óbuda Museum site for current opening times, tickets and any temporary exhibitions.
The Vasarely Museum and the Kassák Museum are in the same Zichy Mansion complex.
An English audio guide for the permanent exhibition is mentioned on the museum's profile; confirm availability on the official site.

historyIntro: Óbuda Museum explores the layered past of the northern Buda district, from its medieval royal days to the 1970s.

historySections.heading: A district older than modern Budapest

children.text: Óbuda incorporates traces of the Roman world alongside later village, town and industrial development. The museum helps explain how separate places came together in the capital formed in 1873.

historySections.heading: Everyday life as a historical source

children.text: Its displays include urban history and collections of objects from ordinary households. The 'Toys in the City' (Játék a városban) exhibition, which the museum calls Budapest's only permanent toy-history exhibition, presents Hungarian toys through the theme of the city.

name: Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives
description: Beside the Dohány Street Synagogue, this museum and archive presents Hungarian Jewish history, ritual objects and the Holocaust. It holds Judaica and what the museum describes as Europe's most comprehensive Jewish community archives, in a 1930s building by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó on the site of Theodor Herzl's birthplace.

children.text: The Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives is at Dohány utca 2, within the complex of the Dohány Street Synagogue in Pest's former Jewish quarter. The synagogue was built in 1854-1859 to plans by Ludwig Förster, with an interior by Frigyes Feszl, and consecrated on 6 September 1859. The museum is attached to it, so a visit puts the building, the memorials and the collections in one place.

The Association of European Jewish Museums says the idea of a separate Jewish exhibition arose during the 1896 millennial celebrations, when Judaism was recognised as one of Hungary's historic religions. The first collection of about 1,500 objects was kept in a downtown apartment. The museum's own building was designed by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó in a style matching the synagogue; sources give 1931 or 1932 for its construction and move-in.

The building stands on the site of Theodor Herzl's birthplace according to Wikipedia. Its collections combine Judaica, everyday and ritual objects and archives. Notable items include a pair of copper rimonim (Torah finials) dated 1602, and a Roman-era gravestone regarded as the oldest trace of the Hungarian Jewish community. According to Wikipedia, the silver trowel used to lay the synagogue's keystone is kept at the museum.

A history of loss runs through the displays. The museum records that in 1942 two employees of the Hungarian National Museum hid the valuable artefacts in a cellar, which is credited with preserving the collection. The collection includes a Holocaust room, and the synagogue complex includes the Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park, where Imre Varga's Tree of Life memorial carries victims' names on its leaves.

The museum and archives were reunited as one institution at the end of 2014. The archives are described as the most comprehensive Jewish community archives in Europe. Because the site is a place of worship, a memorial and a museum, visitors should follow the guidance on dress and behaviour given on the official site.
Good to know
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets, security checks and any dress or head-covering requirements.
The Dohány Street Synagogue, Heroes' Temple and Raoul Wallenberg Memorial Park are in the same complex, so plan enough time for the whole site.
Treat the museum, courtyard and cemetery as places of remembrance: keep voices low and follow staff instructions.

heroImage.alt: The Moorish-style brick facade of the Dohány Street synagogue complex, which includes the Hungarian Jewish Museum

historyIntro: The Hungarian Jewish Museum and Archives preserve objects and records that reveal centuries of Jewish life in Hungary.

historySections.heading: A collection bound to the Jewish Quarter

children.text: The museum is located close to the Dohány Street Synagogue, in an area central to Budapest's Jewish religious and cultural history. Its holdings include objects associated with ritual life, communities, art and documentary memory.

The archival role is especially significant in understanding the Holocaust and the complex continuity of Hungarian Jewish communities before and after it. The institution invites consideration of living traditions as well as loss and remembrance.

name: Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism
description: Founded in 1966 in Buda Castle's former Fortuna Inn, this museum now stands on Korona tér in Óbuda. It follows Hungarian shops, brands, hotels and restaurants from the late 19th century to the Second World War, with recreated interiors and two rooms linked to the writer Gyula Krúdy.

children.text: The Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism is at Korona tér 1 in Óbuda. It was established in 1966 and first worked in the former Fortuna Inn in the Buda Castle district until 2005; the museum has since moved to its present Óbuda address. A profile describes it as the only museum of its kind in the world, with exhibits drawn from across Hungary.

One permanent display, Hosting guests, to be guests, opened on 11 December 2014. It traces Hungarian civilian hospitality from the late 19th century to the Second World War, mainly through room interiors. The title is taken from a 1933 etiquette book by Károly Gundel and Frigyes Karinthy. A separate part of the museum is devoted to trade, with measuring and fairs, and recreated shops such as a sweetshop, an ironmonger's and a stationer's.

Visitors will also find displays on department stores such as the Great Parisian Store and Corvin, and on old brands such as Kajla, Százszorszép and Bambi. An Advertisement Board room shows glazed objects from the trade collection with boards about smoking, drinks and insurance. Touchable objects, drawers to open and touchscreen quizzes make the displays practical for children.

A section titled I have never had a home presents two rooms linked to the writer Gyula Krúdy, who spent his last three years and died in Óbuda. One is furnished as a cheap hotel, and Krúdy's habit of eating in restaurants is reflected in a room furnished as one.

The museum also runs workshops where visitors learn the history of foods such as ice cream or chocolate and then make them, and the building includes the Kultea Theatre, which hosts concerts, book launches, tastings and lectures. Guided tours are available, mostly in English.
Good to know
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and workshop bookings.
Korona tér 1 is in Óbuda (1036); use the BudapestGo planner to find the best way there from your hotel.
Guided tours should be arranged in advance on the official site; most are offered in English.
Combine with the Óbuda Museum, Goldberger Textile Collection and Fő tér, all in the same district.

historyIntro: This museum explores how Hungarian shops, hospitality businesses and visitor culture have shaped everyday life and city streets.

children.text: Trade and hospitality history includes objects easily overlooked elsewhere: shop fittings, signs, menus, packaging, photographs and documents. Together they reveal the changing experiences of customers, staff and travelling visitors.

Budapest's cafés, markets and restaurants are tied to wider changes in urban work and leisure. The museum interprets this world through collections and exhibitions, with themes that may change from one visit to another.
